P=NP means every problem whose solution can be verified in polynomial time can also be solved in polynomial time. But "polynomial time" doesn't mean "solved time == verification time." Polynomial time is a broad category that refers to overall efficiency rather than actual discrete "wall" time.

If the proof yields a fast, concrete algorithm for NP-complete problems, then yes, cryptography as we know it is catastrophically broken. If the proof is nonconstructive or gives something like O(n^1000), then the immediate practical impact may be small for decades.

Every Friday I publish my portfolio. Every position, every entry price, every loss. This autumn that has not been comfortable reading.
 
The book is down around 20% this year. My inflation models underestimated how sticky core prices would be, and an energy shock I expected to fade lasted months longer. Those are my calls, and I'll own them.
 
People sometimes ask why I keep publishing it when it's going badly. Three reasons.
 
First, trust is built in drawdowns, not in rallies. Anyone can share their winners. The useful question for a client, a colleague or an investor is how someone behaves when they're losing, and you can only answer it if they let you see.
 
Second, it keeps me honest about process. When your numbers are public, you can't quietly rewrite the story afterwards. You have to separate the decisions that were wrong from the outcomes that were unlucky, and that discipline makes the next decision better.
 
Third, it is a reminder that certainty is the enemy. The most expensive mistakes I've seen in finance came from people who couldn't change their minds. I'd rather have a system that tells me when the evidence has shifted, even when it's uncomfortable, than a view I'm too proud to drop.
 
That system, for us, is the nowcasting we built at Nowcast IQ, reading growth, inflation and liquidity every day rather than waiting for official releases. It has been wrong at times this year. It is also, right now, telling a very different story from the data the Federal Reserve received this week, and I'll be just as open about whether that turns out to be right.

It strikes me as if those who cannot envision the myriad of ways in which higher (or even just different) forms of intelligences might unlock unpredictable technologies latent in nature fundamentally lack an ability of imagination that requires less than the imagination of a three-year-old.

We already have the evidence for what can reasonably happen. Humans have already unlocked a bountiful load of these latent technologies that drastically altered the conditions for life for every single life form on Earth. Thus, you could ask that it requires almost no imagination at all, that a similar thing could/would happen again, if a different or higher intelligence emerged. 

Humanity is also fully embroiled in the battle with the first-, second- and third-order effects derived from of *our own* discoveries. 

Anyone that has interacted with any modern AI system should atleast be confident to say that the properties of this new mind is that it is significantly faster in some ways, effectively tireless and endlessly parallelizable. Evidently, to such an extent that it can bounce around between disciplines of math to solve the Riemann hypothesis. 

If you gather all these things in your head simultaneously and cannot fathom that the future then quite likely becomes un-navigatable and unpredictable to an existential degree, you surely must lack imagination. 

You cannot even imagine that something that has already occurred on Earth happens, at a different scale, again. You frustratingly belabor the people who possess this level of trivial imagination with the demand: ”Explain to me how all of this AI stuff poses existential risk? Like what are the actual steps?”

The ironic thing is that it is these same minds that will later then question whether AI possesses any true creativity or original thought, any ”true intelligence”, when they so readily demonstrate themselves to lack those exact same qualities through their inability to imagine. It raises the question of whose intelligence it is that is really artificial.

Had a long conversation with Gemini trying to estimate the current rate of discoveries and proofs being generated at the frontier. Gemini picked up so many things I had missed from reading recent papers, references, and revisions. Really just a wonderful model to brainstorm and do detective work with, and so good at grasping intent and going a step ahead without being asked to. Probably the best thought partner in the world right now.

OpenAI generated 700 papers in five weeks last time; they've had seven weeks since then, and the models have become more capable. So from that alone, it was always a safe guess that it was going to be an even bigger release. But it's possible that the rate of discovery has accelerated, for multiple reasons.

It's strange to think about, but the three main labs may be sitting on a staggering amount of novel discoveries right now. The crypto breakthrough dominating recent discourse is just one piece of it, and I think that was discovered near the start of the month. How much they release alongside it is hard to say, but people should brace for far more than they're expecting.
